content.p: On the evening of 9 September 1990, soldiers from an army camp on the edge of Batticaloa in eastern Sri Lanka went through four Tamil villages and told residents to come out onto the road. Most of those taken were women, children and old people. They were told they would be released after questioning. According to Tamil Guardian, 184 of them were killed inside the camp, and other Tamil outlets have since given the toll as 185 or 186. One man, Kanthasamy Krishnakumar, lived to describe it.

No one is reported to have been prosecuted for the killings. What exists is a 1997 inquiry that, according to the outlets reporting it, named three army captains, the testimony of one survivor and a number of relatives, and a long record of memorial events that Tamil Guardian says the authorities have tried to restrict. Nearly all the reporting comes from Tamil-community outlets, so each count and accusation below is credited to whoever made it.

The killings fell in a few violent months. A statement published by Groundviews for the 25th anniversary, after a Batticaloa Peace Committee gathering, said Batticaloa district saw "some of the most brutal violence" of Sri Lanka's long ethnic conflict between June and September 1990. It listed massacres and mass disappearances at Kattankudy, Sathurukondan, Eravur, Kurukkalmadam, Vantharumoolai and Sittandy, and said armed actors from the Sinhala, Tamil and Muslim communities had taken part in the atrocities of that period.
Days before Sathurukondan, on 5 September, Tamil Guardian says, 158 Tamils who had sought refuge at the Eastern University campus were arrested by soldiers and never seen again.

According to Groundviews, armed men in military uniform and in civilian clothes ordered residents of the four villages onto the road at about 5:30 p.m. They were taken to the nearby army camp, which that account calls the Bois Town camp, on the assurance that they would be released after questioning. None of them returned home.

The Sangam.org site put the start of events on 10 September rather than 9 September, a discrepancy the other outlets do not address. It said 185 people were rounded up and marched to the camp, and told that this was a routine inquiry. A witness quoted by the same site, a school principal, described seeing "armed personnel both in civil and military clothing" taking civilians and said he heard cries of distress through the night. Another witness said about 60 soldiers with guns arrived at around 5:30. "I was thinking that they would be released after interrogation," he said, but by eight in the evening they had not come back, and when he went near the camp he heard so many people crying that he went home frightened.

Other relatives gave evidence of how their families were taken. A retired electrical foreman, Augustinepillai Phillippillai, then 73, said his eight-year-old grandson went out to play and was among the crowd led away, and that 19 of his own close relatives were in it. A man whose two sons-in-law had been killed by the army two months earlier said in a statement quoted by Sangam.org that he lost his wife, three daughters and seven grandchildren, among them a one-year-old, eleven members of his family in all. Another witness said his wife had urged him to hide, saying the army would take only the men; she was taken instead.

Only one man is known to have come out alive, according to Tamil Guardian, Countercurrents, Sangam.org and others: Krishnakumar. Countercurrents gives his age as 21. Tamil Guardian reproduces what it says he told TamilNet in 1997. By his account the villages were cordoned off at about 10 a.m., and it was nearly 7 p.m. when the villagers were shut in the camp. Four masked men came into the hall and picked out four of the men, himself among them. They were stripped of their shirts, had their hands tied and were led to the back of the camp, where he saw a pit and a well and about 25 soldiers carrying swords and cudgels.

Krishnakumar said he was struck with a cudgel and then stabbed in the chest and back and thrown into the pit, but did not lose consciousness. He said the soldiers brought more men, then women and girls, and killed them, and that the women were assaulted before they were killed. In the dark he managed to crawl away, hid in scrub behind the camp, and later watched, he said, as soldiers burned the bodies in tyres, a fire that burned until about 3 a.m., before the pit was filled with sand. A passer-by helped him to hospital.

Sangam.org quotes a shorter account from the survivor, in which he says four of them were blindfolded, had cloth stuffed into their mouths and were stabbed with sharp knives, and that he lay as though dead and crawled through the bodies to shrubs at around 3 in the morning. "I lost my whole family in this incident," the account ends. "I am the only survivor." Tamil Guardian quotes its opening line as Krishnakumar's later testimony.

Sangam.org reports what happened next. The army came to the hospital looking for him, and the Batticaloa Peace Committee had him moved to the home of an American Jesuit priest, Father Miller. S. Arunagirinathan, the committee's president and a retired government agent, said it recorded Krishnakumar's testimony and still had the audio. He said the committee took the matter to the Batticaloa brigadier, who refused even to see them, and that more senior officers also declined to discuss it.

Groundviews names a survivor differently. Its account says the outside world learned of the massacre from a survivor called Iraththinaiya, who survived by concealing himself in the reeds on the riverbank, a quarter of a mile away, and who heard the screams of victims while hiding. That account does not mention Krishnakumar, and neither outlet explains whether these are two witnesses or one man described in two ways.

Bishop Kingsley Swamipillai of Trincomalee and Batticaloa, who sat on the Batticaloa Peace Committee, went to the camp the next day with military personnel, Groundviews reported. He told Maatram that everything had been set on fire, but that "there were heads and body parts that were not fully burnt." Colonel Percy Fernando, who went with him, is quoted as saying: "We are very saddened. It is our people who did this. Therefore, I should apologise."

Relatives gave their own accounts of days that followed. Phillippillai said the bishop talked to the brigadier and later went to the camp with members of the citizens' committee, and that one of them, Sivarasa, said afterwards that he saw his wife's slippers and those of many children. The school principal said that the next morning he could not find his uncle, aunt, nephew, niece or any of the children, and saw only some of the children's shoes scattered about. Countercurrents quotes a villager who said that when people went to the camp a week later to ask about missing family members, they were told the people had never come to that area.

The same Countercurrents piece, signed by the secretary of the Tamil Canadian Elders for Human Rights Org, says the military threatened the president of the citizens' committee, Arunakirinathan, and made him sign an affidavit that no such incident had taken place, and that he resigned from his post afterwards. That claim appears in that piece alone.

The figures differ between outlets. The 2015 Tamil Guardian anniversary report gives 184 dead. Countercurrents in 2022 says 185. Later Tamil Guardian reports give 185 or 186, and its report on the families' statement on the 36th anniversary says 186. Groundviews and Sangam.org both say 184.

The Tamil Guardian reports consistently list five children under one, 42 children under ten, nine pregnant women and 28 adults over 68. By village, the 25th-anniversary report gives Sathurukondan 38 dead, Panichchaiyady 37, Pillaiyaradi 62 and Kokuvil 47; a later report counts 39 from Panichchayadi. Sangam.org counts 160 of the 184 as infants, children under ten, elderly people over 60, or eighty-five women, and Countercurrents puts the number of children at 68. These numbers are not the same classification and should not be added together.

President Chandrika Kumaratunga set up a probe in 1997. Tamil Guardian says its retired-judge chairman, whom it names as K. Palakidnar, found strong evidence for the massacre and asked Kumaratunga to hold those responsible to account. It says the inquiry identified three army captains as responsible. Sangam.org calls the chairman Gopala Krishnar. The families' statement on the 36th anniversary says the commission named the principal perpetrators, and that no meaningful action followed on its recommendations. The outlets reporting the inquiry do not name the captains or quote its report.

The officer in charge of the camp, whom Countercurrents calls Captain Gamini Varnakula Sooriya and Sangam.org Captain Gamini Warnakulasooriya, told the inquiry: "On that day no search or arrest was conducted by us." He also said none of his men had left the camp that day. Sangam.org says that every other witness contradicted him.

A TNA MP, Selvam Adaikkalanathan, said at a 2003 memorial event that governments set up commissions of inquiry to "hoodwink" the people and that when a commission came close to the truth it was delayed and then reported without holding anyone accountable. That is his view as reported by Tamil Guardian.
Sangam.org states that none of the perpetrators was ever arrested, charged or punished.
content.h2: Remembering, and the demand for a dig
content.p: The anniversary is marked each year at the memorial in Sathurukondan. Tamil Guardian said that police blocked Tamils from remembering the victims in 2014, and that a remembrance event organised by TNA MPs was halted by a court order. It said that two Batticaloa municipal councillors were summoned by police for marking the 31st anniversary. The outlet describes this as part of a wider pattern of restrictions on Tamil memorials in the north and east; that characterisation is its own.

A survivor who says the whole family was lost lodged a police complaint at Kokkuvil asking for an investigation, Tamil Guardian reported. It says it has long been reported that victims were buried within the camp grounds, and that families and rights groups have asked for the site to be excavated. On the 36th anniversary, relatives called for a forensic excavation of the former camp, carried out with independent international experts, and for a referral of the case to the International Criminal Court or another international accountability body. They said they were gathering "with diminishing hope after 35 years". The outlets do not report any excavation having taken place.
